findings.headline: Your minimum-balance fee is an extreme outlier.
findings.body: At $10.00, your minimum-balance fee is more than 3x the $3.00 median and the highest in the peer group — flagged as an extreme outlier in our data. The sample is small (3 comparable credit unions publish this fee), so the percentile deserves caution, but the direction is clear: you charge the most, on a fee that lands on your lowest-balance members.

findings.headline: The cost of simply holding an account runs double the median.
findings.body: Monthly maintenance is $10.00 against a $5.00 median — the 83rd percentile of 6 comparable credit unions, above the $8.75 75th-percentile mark. Combined with the minimum-balance fee, the two charges tied to just keeping an account open are the only place your schedule prices above market, and they stack on the same members.

findings.headline: Everywhere else, you are at or below market — quietly.
findings.body: NSF runs $15 against a $17.50 peer median and a $25.00 national median. Card replacement is $10 versus a $35 median (26th percentile of 23 peers), cashier's checks $2 versus $5 — the cohort minimum — and paper statements $1 versus $3. On transaction and penalty fees, this is a genuinely member-friendly schedule that no one is talking about.

exec_narrative: Net position: Emblem Federal Credit Union prices penalty and service fees at or below comparable credit unions — NSF under both the peer and national medians, card replacement at less than a third of the going rate, cashier's checks at the cohort minimum — while concentrating its entire above-market posture on the two fees for holding an account: a $10 minimum-balance fee flagged as an extreme outlier and a $10 monthly maintenance fee at double the median. That combination inverts the usual story; it is gentlest on members who make mistakes and hardest on members with small balances. The account-holding fees deserve a deliberate decision, and the member-friendly pricing everywhere else deserves an audience.

callouts.title: Minimum balance fee — $10.00
callouts.stat: Peer median $3.00 · peer max $10.00 · 100th percentile · n=3 · flagged: extreme outlier (>2x median)
callouts.body: You hold the top of the distribution on a fee that, by construction, is paid by members with the least money. Only 3 comparable credit unions publish this fee, so the benchmark is thin — but at more than 3x the median, thinness is not the issue. Whether the answer is a cut, a lower threshold, or a documented rationale, an extreme-outlier flag on a low-balance-member fee is the line most worth a decision.

callouts.title: Monthly maintenance — $10.00
callouts.body: Double the median and above the 75th percentile, and it compounds the minimum-balance exposure: the same small-balance member can face both charges on the same account. Several peers charge $3.50–$5.00. Because this fee recurs monthly, it is also the largest annualized gap on your schedule — roughly $60 a year per affected member versus the median peer.

callouts.title: Penalty and service fees — below market, unmarketed
callouts.stat: NSF $15 vs $17.50 peer / $25.00 national median · Card replacement $10 vs $35 (P26, n=23) · Cashier's check $2 vs $5 (cohort minimum) · Paper statement $1 vs $3
callouts.body: On the fees members fear most — NSF, card replacement — you undercut comparable credit unions decisively, and your NSF fee is $10 under the national median. That is a story your peers' own published schedules substantiate, and it currently appears in no member communication. Rebalancing the account-holding fees would let you tell it without an asterisk.

context_narrative:
Two currents define the fee landscape your schedule competes in. First, the industry-wide retreat from penalty pricing: NSF and overdraft fees have been falling across consumer finance under regulatory and reputational pressure — a shift your $15 NSF fee, below both peer and national medians, is already ahead of. Second, published fee schedules have become marketing documents: public, scraped, and compared, which means an extreme-outlier flag on any line is a small reputational bet, and a below-market line unadvertised is an asset left idle.

Mid-sized credit unions occupy an exposed middle: large enough to show up in fee comparisons alongside banks and bigger credit unions, without the marketing reach to shape the narrative afterward. For an institution already member-friendly on penalties and services, the highest-leverage move is narrow — rework the two account-holding fees that concentrate cost on small-balance members, then lead member communications with the pricing the rest of the schedule already earns.
